claim: The TREM2 crystal structure was determined at 3.1 Å resolution.
source: We determined the crystal structure of the TREM2 ectodomain at 3.1 Å resolution
evidence: The resolution is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by crystallographic data in the methods and results sections.

claim: Nasu-Hakola disease mutations in TREM2 are buried within the protein structure.
source: The side chains of mutations causing NHD (Y38, T66 and V126) are all buried within the core of the Ig fold
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and solvent accessibility calculations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Alzheimer's disease risk variants in TREM2 are found on the protein surface.
source: the side chains of verified AD risk variants (R47H and R62H) and possible AD risk variants (N68K, D87N and T96K) all lie on the protein surface
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and solvent accessibility calculations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nasu-Hakola disease mutations impact TREM2 protein stability and decrease folded TREM2 surface expression.
source: Biophysical and cellular methods indicate that Nasu-Hakola mutations impact protein stability and decrease folded TREM2 surface expression
evidence: This is supported by SEC analysis, flow cytometry, and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Alzheimer's disease risk variants impact binding to a TREM2 ligand.
source: Alzheimer's risk variants impact binding to a TREM2 ligand
evidence: This is supported by cell binding assays using TREM2 tetramers and monomeric proteins shown in Figure 4.

claim: The TREM2 R47H variant is associated with Alzheimer's disease risk similar to that associated with APOE4.
source: In particular, the TREM2 R47H variant is associated with a risk that is similar to that associated with APOE4, previously the only well-established risk factor for late-onset AD.
evidence: This is based on genetic sequencing studies cited in the introduction.

claim: The TREM2 R47H mutation correlates with increased cerebrospinal fluid tau levels.
source: This mutation correlates with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau levels, a well-established risk factor for AD (Cruchaga et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cruchaga et al., 2013.

claim: TREM2 is an innate immune receptor expressed on dendritic cells, resident macrophages, infiltrating macrophages, inflammatory macrophages, and CSF monocytes.
source: TREM2 is an innate immune receptor expressed on dendritic cells (DCs), resident macrophages such as osteoclasts and microglia, infiltrating (Jay et al., 2015) and inflammatory (Wu et al., 2015) macrophages, and CSF monocytes (Colonna and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: TREM2 is a type one receptor protein consisting of an extracellular V-type Ig domain, a short stalk, a transmembrane domain that associates with DAP12, and a cytoplasmic tail.
source: It is a type one receptor protein consisting of an extracellular V-type Ig domain, a short stalk, a transmembrane domain that associates with the adaptor protein DAP12 for signaling, and a cytoplasmic tail (Figure 1a) (Colonna, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia.
source: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia, and the absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, which was correlated with increased accumulation of Aβ plaques (Wang et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015 and Jay et al., 2015.

claim: The absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis.
source: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia, and the absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, which was correlated with increased accumulation of Aβ plaques (Wang et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015 and Jay et al., 2015.

claim: Microglia in TREM2-deficient AD mice do not engulf Aβ plaques.
source: Microglia in TREM2-deficient AD mice displayed less activation and did not engulf Aβ plaques.
evidence: This is based on observations from AD mouse model studies cited in the introduction.

claim: The TREM2 ectodomain contains two disulfide bonds: one between C36 and C110, and another between C51 and C60.
source: The TREM2 ectodomain is a V-type Ig domain containing two disulfide bonds, the canonical Ig disulfide between residues C36 and C110 (βB–βF) and an additional linkage between C51 and C60 (βC-βC') (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A single N-acetylglucosamine glycan is present at residue N79 in the TREM2 structure.
source: A single N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) glycan that remains after Endo Hf treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) is clearly visible in the electron density at residue N79 (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density maps shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The Y38C mutation in TREM2 most likely disrupts correct disulfide formation.
source: Y38 is adjacent to C36, which forms an intramolecular disulfide with C110, so the Y38C mutation most likely disrupts correct disulfide formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the Y38 position relative to the disulfide bond.

claim: The T66M mutation would sterically disrupt packing and probably destabilize the TREM2 protein.
source: The T66M mutation would sterically disrupt this packing and probably destabilize the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of T66's position and interactions.

claim: The V126G mutation would disrupt hydrophobic core packing and probably destabilize TREM2.
source: Removal of the side chain by the V126G mutation would disrupt this packing and probably destabilize this hydrophobic core (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of V126's position in the hydrophobic core.

claim: Y38 and V126 are conserved within the TREM family.
source: In addition, sequence analysis reveals that Y38 and V126 are conserved within the TREM family, implying that they are probably required to preserve the common fold within this family of receptors (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Wild-type human TREM2 ectodomain elutes as a monomer in size exclusion chromatography.
source: WT hTREM2 ectodomain consistently eluted as a monomer (Figure 2a and b)
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: AD-risk variants (R47H, R62H, N68K, D87N, T96K) elute at the same volume as WT TREM2 in size exclusion chromatography.
source: The verified (R47H and R62H) and possible (N68K, D87N and T96K) AD-risk variants all elute at the same volume as WT TREM2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–l)
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–l.

claim: NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G elute much earlier than WT TREM2, consistent with aggregation and misfolding.
source: By contrast, although the buried NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G were secreted, they elute much earlier, consistent with aggregation and misfolding of these proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1m–o).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1m–o.

claim: TREM2 NHD mutant ectodomains are largely produced as covalent dimers or trimers under non-reducing conditions.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of TREM2 NHD mutants in the absence of reducing agent showed that these ectodomains were largely produced as covalent dimers or trimers, indicating that misfolding of these mutants promoted the formation of aberrant intermolecular disulfide bonds (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Anti-TREM2 staining is decreased for NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G but not for AD risk variants.
source: However, as predicted by our structural analysis, anti-TREM2 staining was decreased for the NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G, but not for the AD risk variants R47H, R62H, N68K, D87N, and T96K (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Anti-FLAG antibody shows surface expression for all TREM2 mutants.
source: By contrast, the anti-FLAG antibody showed surface expression for all TREM2 mutants (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The R47H variant has an altered CD spectrum compared to WT TREM2.
source: We found that R62H and T96K displayed CD spectra similar to WT proteins while, surprisingly, R47H showed a subtle, yet statistically significant difference in the 214 nm/233 nm ratio (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: The R47H mutation in TREM2 induces a small, but measurable, conformational change.
source: Thus the R47H mutation in TREM2 seems to induce a small, but measurable, conformational change, whereas the R62H and T96K mutations do not induce any structural changes detectable by CD.
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: AD surface variants produce slightly lower denaturation temperatures than WT TREM2 as measured by DSF.
source: Each surface variant produced slightly lower denaturation temperatures, with R47H and R62H marginally reduced when compared to WT proteins and T96K having the lowest denaturation temperatures (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DSF data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: WT TREM2 and all TREM2 variants tested show reversible thermal denaturation.
source: WT TREM2 and all the TREM2 variants tested showed reversible thermal denaturation as they reacquired their native spectra rapidly after cooling from 90°C to 20°C
evidence: This is demonstrated by CD thermal denaturation experiments.

claim: The ability of TREM2 variants to refold after thermal denaturation is ablated in the presence of DTT.
source: WT TREM2 and all the TREM2 variants tested showed reversible thermal denaturation as they reacquired their native spectra rapidly after cooling from 90°C to 20°C, but their ability to refold was ablated in the presence of DTT (not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CD thermal denaturation experiments with DTT.

claim: The T96K variant has a pronounced shift towards lower denaturation temperature compared to WT TREM2.
source: In contrast to DSF measurements, thermal denaturation by CD did not show a difference between WT, R47H, and R62H proteins; however, the T96K variant has a pronounced shift towards lower denaturation temperature (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CD thermal denaturation data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: R47H and R62H proteins melt at slightly lower GuHCl concentrations than WT TREM2.
source: The R47H and R62H proteins melt at slightly lower GuHCl concentrations than the WT protein, while the T96K variant unfolds at lower GuHCl concentrations than R47H and R62H, consistent with the thermal melt experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemical denaturation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: TREM2 was shown to signal following stimulation of reporter cells by plated phospholipids.
source: Recently, TREM2 was shown to signal following stimulation of reporter cells by plated phospholipids, and the R47H mutation resulted in loss of signaling (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: TREM2 binds to phospholipids as detected by ELISA and liposome sedimentation assays.
source: Consistent with the results of previous work (Cannon et al., 2012), we detected TREM2 binding to phospholipids by both ELISA and liposome sedimentation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA and liposome sedimentation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No differences in phospholipid discrimination or direct lipid binding were observed between WT and AD variant TREM2 ectodomains.
source: However, we did not observe differences in phospholipid discrimination or in direct lipid binding between WT and AD variant TREM2 ectodomains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phospholipid binding assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: Human and mouse TREM2/SA-PE tetramers bind to Neuro2A and THP-1 cells.
source: In initial experiments, we found that both human and mouse TREM2/SA-PE tetramers were able to bind Neuro2A (N2A) and THP-1 cells (Figure 4b–d,f,g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Overnight treatment with PMA/ionomycin dramatically decreases binding of TREM2/SA-PE tetramers to THP-1 cells.
source: To validate the specificity of our reagent, we cultured THP-1 cells with various immune stimuli and found that overnight treatment with PMA/ionomycin dramatically decreased binding of TREM2/SA-PE tetramers to THP-1 cells (Figure 4b and c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: TREM2 binding to cells is sensitive to proteinase treatment.
source: We next sought to interrogate the endogenous target recognized by TREM2 on the cell surface, and found that TREM2 binding is sensitive to proteinase treatment of cells prior to incubation with our staining reagent (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Treatment with proteinase K abolished TREM2 binding to cells.
source: Treatment with proteinase K abolished binding while the more specific proteases chymotrypsin and elastase had an intermediate effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: TREM2-L contains a protein component.
source: This demonstrates that TREM2-L contains a protein component.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteinase sensitivity experiments.

claim: GAG-dependent cell binding of the TREM2 tetramer was observed in CHO cells.
source: We tested binding to wild-type CHO-K1 cells, which express heparan and chondroitin sulfates, and to CHO-745 cells, which are deficient in GAG maturation and surface expression (Esko et al., 1985). In this experiment, GAG-dependent cell binding of the TREM2 tetramer was observed (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Treatment with heparinases had a pronounced effect on TREM2 cell surface binding.
source: In CHO (Figure 4e), THP-1 (Figure 4f) and N2A (Figure 4g) cells, treatment with heparinases had a pronounced effect on cell surface binding while chondroitinase only slightly diminished binding
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4e, f, and g.

claim: Heparin sulfate is a major component of the cell surface TREM2-L.
source: In CHO (Figure 4e), THP-1 (Figure 4f) and N2A (Figure 4g) cells, treatment with heparinases had a pronounced effect on cell surface binding while chondroitinase only slightly diminished binding, together implicating GAGs, specifically heparin sulfate, as a major component of the cell surface TREM2-L.
evidence: This is inferred from the heparinase treatment experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The AD-linked variant R47H displayed markedly diminished binding to N2A and THP-1 cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the AD-linked variant R47H displayed markedly diminished binding to N2A and THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The T96K variant significantly increased binding to TREM2-L on cells.
source: In stark contrast, the potentially AD-protective T96K variant significantly increased binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The R62H variant reduced binding to TREM2-L as measured in the anti-6H format.
source: The R62H variant reduced binding as measured in the anti-6H format, but the reduction in binding was less dramatic when measured by competition or tetramer staining, suggesting an intermediate decrease in affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: TREM2 has a large basic surface that is not present on other TREM family receptors.
source: Upon mapping the electrostatic surface of hTREM2, we noticed a large basic surface that was not present on the surface of other TREM family receptors for which coordinates are available (mTREM1, PDB 1 U9K, [Kelker et al., 2004a]; hTREM1, PDB 1SMO, [Kelker et al., 2004b]; and TLT-1, PDB 2FRG [Gattis et al., 2006]) (Figure 5a,b and d–f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrostatic surface analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The residues constituting the basic patch on TREM2 are highly conserved within TREM2 but not within the rest of the TREM family.
source: Furthermore, sequence analysis shows that the residues constituting this basic patch are highly conserved within TREM2, but not within the rest of the TREM family, suggesting that this interface has evolved specifically toward a role in TREM2 function (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: TREM2 ectodomain tetramers bind to N2A cells while TREML2 and TREML4 tetramers do not.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, TREM2 ectodomain tetramers bound to N2A cells, while tetramers of ectodomains from TREM-like 2 (TREML2) and TREM-like 4 (TREML4) did not (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: R76D and R77D mutations decrease binding to TREM2-L on THP-1 cells.
source: We found that both a R76D and a R77D mutation decreased binding to TREM2-L on THP-1 cells in a manner similar to the validated AD risk variants (R47H and R62H) (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The basic surface on TREM2 represents a conserved functional interface that participates in cell-surface ligand binding.
source: Together, the data indicate that this surface represents a conserved functional interface on TREM2 that participates in cell-surface ligand binding and that this surface is unique to TREM2 within the TREM family.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and binding experiments.

claim: NHD mutations are homozygous and lead to complete loss of TREM2 function.
source: In NHD, the mutations are homozygous and the TREM2 is either deleted or misfolded, leading to a complete loss of function, and more serious and early-onset neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis and the observed effects of NHD mutations.

claim: AD mutations are heterozygous and impair but do not completely abolish TREM2 function.
source: In AD, the mutations are heterozygous and impair function (but do not completely abolish it), leading to less severe and late onset neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis and the observed effects of AD risk variants.

claim: Heterozygous NHD variants have been reported in rare AD cases.
source: Consistent with this, there have been reports of rare AD cases containing heterozygous NHD variants, including Q33X, Y38C, and T66M (Guerreiro et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guerreiro et al., 2013b.

claim: Soluble TREM2 may be a survival signal in bone-marrow macrophages.
source: We have recently shown that the soluble TREM2 may be a survival signal in bone-marrow macrophages (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2015.

claim: The absence of TREM2 in an AD mouse model prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, we have observed that the absence of TREM2 in an AD mouse model prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, suggesting that soluble TREM2 could play a similar role in the CNS (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Soluble TREM2 can be detected in the CNS.
source: Accordingly, soluble TREM2 can be detected in the CNS, and we have shown that some AD risk variants, but not the NHD mutant proteins are readily detected in the CSF of patients (Piccio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Piccio et al., 2016.

claim: Some AD risk variants, but not NHD mutant proteins, are readily detected in the CSF of patients.
source: Accordingly, soluble TREM2 can be detected in the CNS, and we have shown that some AD risk variants, but not the NHD mutant proteins are readily detected in the CSF of patients (Piccio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Piccio et al., 2016.

claim: The TREM2 ectodomain contains nine β-strands characteristic of V-type Ig domains.
source: The nine β-strands characteristic of proteins within this Ig domain class are present, and two short α-helix passages are observed spanning β-sheets B–C and E–F.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The TREM2 asymmetric unit contains two monomers in a parallel arrangement.
source: The asymmetric unit (ASU) contains two monomers of hTREM2 in a parallel arrangement, but the limited buried surface area (~400 Å2) and chemical nature of the interface suggest that this dimer would not exist in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The two TREM2 monomers in the asymmetric unit are quite similar with a Cα RMSD of 0.65 Å.
source: Furthermore, these two monomers are quite similar (Cα RMSD of 0.65 Å, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: R47 side chain lies parallel along the surface of the protein and engages the carbonyl oxygen of T66.
source: R47, the residue with the strongest link to AD as the R47H variant, is at the end of the loop preceding β-sheet C. It is well-ordered in the structure with the side chain lying parallel along the surface of the protein, and the side-chain amines engage the carbonyl oxygen of T66 (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1e.

claim: T96 side chain points away from the surface and engages the side chain of Q33.
source: T96 is on the end of β-strand E and its side chain points away from the surface and engages the side chain of Q33 (Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1g.

claim: NHD mutant Y38C displays diffuse intracellular accumulation in permeabilized cells.
source: We found that the surface expression pattern in non-permeabilized cells was similar for all cell types, whereas in permeabilized cells, the NHD mutant Y38C displayed diffuse intracellular accumulation, in comparison to WT and R47H which displayed a distinct punctate staining pattern (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Significant amounts of SDS-resistant aggregates are found when expressing full-length TREM2 NHD mutants in 293T cells.
source: Consistent with these observations, we found significant amounts of SDS-resistant aggregates by anti-FLAG immunoblotting when expressing the full-length TREM2 NHD mutants in 293T cells (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Both Y38C and R47H variants have some signaling potential but neither sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2.
source: Consistent with our observation of FLAG-TREM2 on the cell surface for all the variant proteins, we found that while both the Y38C and R47H variants have some signaling potential, as assessed by phosphorylated-ERK blotting in RAW264.7 and Cos-7 cells, neither of these variants sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2 (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phospho-ERK immunoblot data shown in Figure 2i and j.

claim: TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic over neutral lipids.
source: In contrast to highly selective phospholipid binding by other Ig domains (Kobayashi et al., 2007; Miyanishi et al., 2007; Santiago et al., 2007; Simhadri et al., 2012), purified TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic (PA, PG, PI, PS) over more neutral (PC, PE) lipids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b and c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipid ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA.
source: Moreover, while TREM2 does share a conserved aspartic acid residue from this motif, which chelates a required Ca2+ ion for the TIM and CD300a proteins, TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA, unlike TIM and CD300 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e and f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipid ELISA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: TREM2 does not bind apoptotic Jurkat T cells which present PS on their cell surface.
source: This is potentially supported by a recent report that TREM2 binds to isolated PS, but does not bind apoptotic Jurkat T cells, which present PS on their cell surface but may also be deficient in GAGs (Bailey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bailey et al., 2015.

claim: TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE.
source: On that note, while this manuscript was in preparation, it was reported that TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE and that this interaction facilitates uptake of Aβ loaded into lipoparticles by microglia (Yeh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeh et al., 2016.

claim: TREM2 AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE.
source: This report also suggests that TREM2 AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE, but binding affinities were not quantitated.
evidence: This is based on the report by Yeh et al., 2016.

claim: TREM2 can specifically bind GAGs utilizing the basic patch.
source: Our study demonstrates that TREM2 can specifically bind GAGs, utilizing the basic patch; other TREM-like proteins with the same overall calculated pI, but lacking the basic patch residues, do not bind GAGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry experiments comparing TREM2, TREML2, and TREML4.

claim: TREM2 AD risk variants affect binding to GAGs.
source: We also demonstrate that TREM2 AD risk variants affect binding to GAGs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry experiments with TREM2 variants.

claim: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability, which was >99% by 7-AAD staining.
source: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability, which was >99% by 7-aminoactinomycin D (7-AAD) staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry viability analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2f.

claim: The T96 residue is less conserved in the TREM family but is highly conserved in TREM2 proteins across species.
source: The T66 residue is less conserved in the TREM family, but is highly conserved in TREM2 proteins across species.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing the production of inflammatory cytokines.
source: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing the production of inflammatory cytokines from bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and dendritic cells (BMDDCs) in response to FcR (Hamerman et al., 2006) and Tlr signaling (Turnbull et al., 2006; Ito and Hamerman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TREM2 participates in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells in cultured microglia and reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Likewise, TREM2 participates in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells in cultured microglia and reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines (Takahashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2005.

claim: TREM2-expressing macrophages can promote inflammatory disease in the brain and lung.
source: However, TREM2-expressing macrophages can also promote inflammatory disease in the brain (Jay et al., 2015) and lung (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jay et al., 2015 and Wu et al., 2015.

claim: Several classes of molecules have been proposed as TREM2 ligands, including bacterial carbohydrates, sulfoglycolipids, nucleic acids, phospholipids, and proteins.
source: The identity of a physiologic TREM2 ligand (TREM2-L) remains uncertain, although several classes of molecules have been proposed, including bacterial carbohydrates (Daws et al., 2003; Quan et al., 2008), sulfoglycolipids (Phongsisay et al., 2015), nucleic acids (Kawabori et al., 2015), phospholipids (Cannon et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015) and proteins (Stefano et al., 2009; Takegahara et al., 2006; Yoon et al., 2012; Atagi et al., 2015; Bailey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Cells that express a TREM2-L include astrocytes, DCs, BMDMs, neurons, and apoptotic cells.
source: Additionally, previous studies have identified cells that express a TREM2-L, including astrocytes (Daws et al., 2003), DCs (Ito and Hamerman, 2012), BMDMs (Hamerman et al., 2006), neurons and apoptotic cells (Hsieh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Microglia-specific networks, including those containing TREM2, are most significantly dysregulated in late-onset AD.
source: A recent study of more than 1,600 late-onset AD (LOAD) and cognitively normal brains revealed that microglia-specific networks, including those containing TREM2, are those most significantly dysregulated in LOAD (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: The TREM2 R47H mutation has been identified in patients with frontal temporal dementia, Parkinson's disease, and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: This mutation correlates with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau levels, a well-established risk factor for AD (Cruchaga et al., 2013), and subsequent studies have identified this mutation in patients who have frontal temporal dementia (FTD), Parkinson's disease (PD) (Rayaprolu et al., 2013), and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Cady et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Homozygous TREM2 mutations including early-stop codons, splice site mutations, coding stalk mutations D134G and K186N, and coding ectodomain mutations Y38C, T66M, and V126G cause NHD or a frontotemporal dementia variant.
source: Homozygous mutations including early-stop codons (Paloneva et al., 2003; Soragna et al., 2003), splice site mutations (Numasawa et al., 2011; Chouery et al., 2008), the coding stalk mutations D134G and K186N (Paloneva et al., 2002), and the coding ectodomain mutations Y38C, T66M, and V126G (Guerreiro et al., 2013a, 2013c; Le Ber et al., 2014) cause either NHD, characterized by early-onset dementia, demyelination, and bone cyst lipoma (Paloneva et al., 2002; Colonna, 2003), or a frontotemporal dementia variant with severe loss of brain matter but lacking the bone manifestations.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The coding mutation R62H is associated with increased risk of AD in independent studies.
source: In addition to R47H, the coding mutation R62H is associated with increased risk of AD in independent studies (Jin et al., 2014; Ridge et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2014 and Ridge et al., 2016.

claim: N68K and D87N have been identified in AD patients, but their risk remains uncertain due to rarity.
source: N68K and D87N have also been identified in AD patients, but because these mutations are very rare, their risk remains uncertain (Guerreiro et al., 2013b; Jonsson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guerreiro et al., 2013b and Jonsson et al., 2013.

claim: The mutation T96K has been linked to a decreased risk of AD, but this mutation is too rare to allow verification.
source: In addition, the mutation T96K has been linked to a decreased risk of AD, but this mutation is also too rare to allow verification of this observation (Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jin et al., 2014.

claim: Diffuse Aβ structures are more neurotoxic than dense Aβ plaques.
source: This impacts the density of Aβ plaques and promotes diffuse Aβ structures, which in turn are more neurotoxic, and contributes to the accumulation of classic AD pathology (Wang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016 and Yuan et al., 2016.
